claims.paper: §3.1 (winter oxygen paragraph; proposed addition, brief Phase 5)
claims.claim: winter (under-ice) oxygen depletion rate per unit volume falls with mean depth
claims.location: p. 185 (PDF p. 45), abstract; p. 187 (PDF p. 47), Results; p. 188 (PDF p. 48), Fig. 1
claims.quote: Volume-based oxygen consumption in ice-covered lakes shows a strong inverse correlation with mean depth
claims.conditions: four sets of Canadian lakes (10 prairie pothole lakes in Manitoba, 16 southeastern Ontario lakes, Arctic lakes from Welch 1974, Experimental Lakes Area lakes); rates in g O2 per m3 of whole-lake volume at freeze-up per day, against mean depth under ice (m); the relation has the form Y = 1/X, i.e. a constant areal rate, and lines for 0.40 and 0.08 g O2 m-2 d-1 'encompass almost the entire range of data points' (p. 187); at small mean depth rates differ 5-fold between productive and unproductive lakes
claims.note: the authors stress that mean depth alone is 'strictly empirical' and cannot separate productive from unproductive lakes (p. 187); they replace it with the sediment area : volume ratio (next claim)

claims.paper: §3.1 (winter oxygen paragraph; proposed addition, brief Phase 5)
claims.claim: winter oxygen depletion rate is a linear function of the ratio of sediment area to lake volume, with a steeper slope in eutrophic than in oligotrophic lakes
claims.location: p. 189 (PDF p. 49), Fig. 2 and its regression equations; p. 190 (PDF p. 50), 'The sediment area: lake volume ratio'
claims.quote: sediment area:lake volume ratio accounts for 72 and 78% of the variation
claims.conditions: Fig. 2 regressions (read on the page image): eutrophic lakes y = 0.226x + 0.010, oligotrophic lakes y = 0.075x + 0.012, y = winter O2 depletion rate (g m-3 d-1), x = sediment area / lake volume (m2 m-3), both ice-corrected; r2 = 0.72 (eutrophic) and 0.78 (oligotrophic); slopes differ (P < 0.01); x spans about 0.02-0.86 m2 m-3; eutrophic = the prairie lakes (summer chlorophyll a 13.6-102), fertilized ELA lakes 227 and 261, ELA 304, Meretta, Water and Severson lakes; oligotrophic = Ontario, most ELA and Arctic lakes
claims.note: since A/V is the inverse of mean depth, the slopes are the sediments' areal O2 uptake; the intercepts (~0.01 g m-3 d-1) are water-column respiration, not significantly different from 0 (p. 191)

claims.paper: §3.1 (winter oxygen paragraph; proposed addition, brief Phase 5)
claims.claim: under ice, eutrophic lake sediments consume about 0.23 g O2 m-2 d-1 and oligotrophic sediments about 0.08 (0.075), while water-column respiration is about 0.01 g O2 m-3 d-1 in both
claims.location: p. 185 (PDF p. 45), abstract; p. 188 (PDF p. 48), Results; p. 191 (PDF p. 51), 'Water column respiration'
claims.quote: oligotrophic lakes consume oxygen at a mean rate of 0.075
claims.conditions: the slopes of the Fig. 2 regressions; winter (ice-covered) rates over the linear part of the depletion curve (mean D.O. above ~3 mg/L); the abstract rounds 0.075 to 0.08 g m-2 d-1

claims.paper: §3.1 (winter oxygen paragraph, 'falling to 20-50 % of the initial rate by late winter'; proposed addition)
claims.claim: the depletion rate slows once oxygen runs low: below a whole-lake mean of about 3.8 mg/L consumption is limited by oxygen supply to the sediments
claims.location: p. 185 (PDF p. 45), abstract; p. 191 (PDF p. 51), 'Limiting oxygen concentration'; p. 192 (PDF p. 52)
claims.quote: limited by oxygen supply below an average whole-lake oxygen concentration of 3.8
claims.conditions: prairie lakes only (shallow, eutrophic); the depletion curves become curvilinear below about 3.0 mg/L mean D.O.; above a near-sediment D.O. of 3-4 g m-3 sediment respiration is roughly constant; 2.1 g m-3 at 30 cm above the sediment corresponds to a whole-lake mean of 3.8 g m-3; computed eddy diffusion near the sediments 3.72 +/- 1.41 x 10-3 cm2 s-1 (minimum values)
claims.note: management implication stated on p. 192: below ~3.8 mg/L, mixing under intact ice 'should effectively hasten the onset of anoxia'

notes: Project arithmetic for the rewrite (not in the source): with A/V = 1/mean depth, Upper's published mean depth 3.35 m gives A/V 0.30 m-1 and, from the Fig. 2 lines, 0.034 mg/L/d (oligotrophic line) to 0.078 mg/L/d (eutrophic line); with ~0.5 m of ice (2.85 m under ice) 0.038-0.089 mg/L/d; over 145 days of ice 5.0-5.6 mg/L (oligotrophic) and 11-13 mg/L (eutrophic) removed from the mean column. Lower (2.55 m) gives 0.041-0.099 mg/L/d. The paper's current estimate from Schwefel et al. 2023 (abstract only) is 0.06-0.12 mg/L/d; Mathias & Barica's areal envelope (0.08-0.40 g m-2 d-1, Fig. 1) contains Schwefel's 0.2-0.39. Caveats: the rates are per m3 of volume at freeze-up (not corrected for ice; p. 186) while A/V is ice-corrected; their 'oligotrophic' lakes are Shield and Arctic lakes, and Hot Brook's trophic state lies between the two lines; the oxygen-limitation threshold (3.8 mg/L) is from shallow prairie lakes only. Also on p. 186: in Barica & Mathias (1979), the prairie lakes' areal winter depletion correlated with mean depth (r = 0.92) but not with chlorophyll or nutrients; Welch et al. (1976) found mean depth the strongest correlate for 16 Ontario lakes. The issue PDF (49 MB) is kept whole; getsrc indexed only pp. 45-54.
